value.question: What is the diameter of the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror, and in which year was it launched?

steps.description: Search the web for the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror diameter and launch year from technical/primary sources.
Fetch relevant pages (e.g., NASA or ESA official pages) to confirm both the mirror diameter and launch year.

key_findings: Webb's primary mirror is 6.5 meters (21 feet 4 inches) across, made of 18 hexagonal mirror segments (each 1.32 meters flat-to-flat), according to the NASA 'Webb's Mirrors' page (web-724f86a54cbd) and corroborated by the Wikipedia page (web-32a538d8c233, 6.5-meter diameter) and NASA's launch article (web-a254efe25db8, 21.3 foot / 6.5 meter primary mirror).

Webb was launched on December 25, 2021, on board an Ariane 5 rocket from Europe's Spaceport (ELA-3) in Kourou, French Guiana, per the NASA 'Webb's Launch' pages (fetch-7fea64a6bc3a and web-40fc69c97a06) and NASA's launch news release (web-a254efe25db8).
gaps: One NASA press release (web-5c1b545fb545) refers to a planned launch date of December 18, 2021, which was a target date that was superseded; the evidence consistently confirms the actual launch as December 25, 2021.
The evidence does not address whether 'diameter' refers to the overall primary mirror aperture (6.5 m) versus the individual segment size (1.32 m each) beyond stating both figures explicitly.

value.text: The James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror is 6.5 meters (21 feet 4 inches) across, composed of 18 hexagonal beryllium segments, each 1.32 meters flat-to-flat alert. This makes it the largest primary mirror ever launched into space. The telescope was launched on December 25, 2021, on board an Ariane 5 rocket from Europe's Spaceport at Kourou, French Guiana, as part of the European Space Agency's contribution to the mission. The launch date and mirror size are confirmed across NASA's official mission pages and NASA's launch news release.

Webb's Mirrors

Overview

One of the James Webb Space Telescope's science goals is to look back through time to when galaxies were young. Webb does this by observing galaxies that are very distant, at over 13 billion light years away from us. To see such far-off and faint objects, Webb needs a large mirror. A telescope’s sensitivity, or how much detail it can see, is directly related to the size of the mirror area that collects light from the objects being observed.
